IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_customer')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_customer');
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_seller')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_seller');
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_product')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_product');
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_date')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_date');


CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_customer
WITH (LOCATION = 'dim_customer/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS customer_key, *
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, customer_unique_id, customer_city, customer_state, customer_zip_code_prefix
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_customers_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS c
) AS c;

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_seller
WITH (LOCATION = 'dim_seller/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY seller_id) AS seller_key, *
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT seller_id, seller_city, seller_state, seller_zip_code_prefix
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_sellers_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS s
) AS s;

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_product
WITH (LOCATION = 'dim_product/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY product_id) AS product_key, *
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT p.product_id, p.product_category_name, t.product_category_name_english,
           p.product_weight_g, p.product_length_cm, p.product_height_cm, p.product_width_cm
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_products_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS p
    LEFT JOIN OPENROWSET(BULK 'product_category_name_translation', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS t
        ON p.product_category_name = t.product_category_name
) AS p;

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_date
WITH (
    LOCATION = 'dim_date/',
    DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake,
    FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff
)
AS
SELECT *
FROM OPENROWSET(
    BULK 'dim_date_seed/',
    DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake',
    FORMAT = 'DELTA'
) AS rows;

IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'fact_order_items')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE fact_order_items');
    
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE fact_order_items
WITH (LOCATION = 'fact_order_items/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY oi.order_id, oi.order_item_id) AS order_item_key,
    dc.customer_key, dp.product_key, ds.seller_key, dd.date_key as order_date_key,
    oi.order_id, oi.order_item_id, oi.price, oi.freight_value,
    pay.total_payment_value, rev.avg_review_score
FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_order_items_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS oi
JOIN OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_orders_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS o
    ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN dim_customer dc ON o.customer_id = dc.customer_id
JOIN dim_product dp ON oi.product_id = dp.product_id
JOIN dim_seller ds ON oi.seller_id = ds.seller_id
JOIN dim_date dd ON CAST(o.order_purchase_timestamp AS DATE) = dd.Date
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(payment_value) AS total_payment_value
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_order_payments_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS p
    GROUP BY order_id
) pay ON oi.order_id = pay.order_id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, AVG(TRY_CAST(review_score AS FLOAT)) AS avg_review_score
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_order_reviews_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS r
    GROUP BY order_id
) rev ON oi.order_id = rev.order_id;

/* ============================================================
   GOLD LAYER — DIMENSION TABLES
   Olist E-Commerce Analytics Project

   Purpose: builds the Gold-layer star schema dimensions from
   the cleaned Silver-layer Delta tables, using Synapse serverless
   SQL's CETAS (CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE AS SELECT) — the only way
   to persist query results in a serverless pool, since it has
   no native storage of its own and no INSERT/UPDATE support.

   Each dimension gets a surrogate key (a simple, stable integer)
   generated via ROW_NUMBER(), rather than relying on the natural
   business keys (customer_id, product_id, etc.) directly — this
   is standard Kimball-style dimensional modeling practice and
   keeps the fact table's foreign keys small and consistent.
   ============================================================ */

USE db_olist_gold;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   One-time setup (run once per environment, then leave commented
   out — re-running CREATE on an object that already exists errors)
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   - EXTERNAL DATA SOURCE: named shortcuts pointing at the Silver
     and Gold containers in ADLS Gen2, so later statements can
     reference 'silver_lake' / 'gold_lake' instead of full URLs.
   - EXTERNAL FILE FORMAT: tells CETAS to write its output as
     Parquet (CETAS always writes Parquet, regardless of what
     format the source data was in).

CREATE EXTERNAL DATA SOURCE silver_lake
WITH (LOCATION = 'abfss://silver@stolistdevweu.dfs.core.windows.net/');

CREATE EXTERNAL DATA SOURCE gold_lake
WITH (LOCATION = 'abfss://gold@stolistdevweu.dfs.core.windows.net/');

CREATE EXTERNAL FILE FORMAT parquet_ff
WITH (FORMAT_TYPE = PARQUET);
*/

/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   Drop existing tables before rebuilding, so this script can be
   re-run safely (e.g. by the automated pipeline) without manual
   cleanup. Synapse serverless SQL's DROP EXTERNAL TABLE does NOT
   support "IF EXISTS" directly, so we check sys.external_tables
   first and only drop when the table is actually there.

   Note: dropping the table only removes SQL's metadata pointer —
   it does NOT delete the underlying Parquet files in storage.
   The pipeline's cleanup step handles clearing those separately
   before this script runs, so CETAS doesn't hit a "location
   already exists" error below.
   ------------------------------------------------------------ */
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_customer')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_customer');
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_seller')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_seller');
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_product')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_product');
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'dim_date')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE dim_date');


/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   dim_customer
   One row per unique customer. Reads directly from the cleaned
   Silver Delta table via OPENROWSET; DISTINCT guards against any
   duplicate rows slipping through, and ROW_NUMBER() generates a
   deterministic surrogate key ordered by the natural key
   (customer_id), avoiding the non-determinism risk that comes
   from ordering by a non-unique column.
   ------------------------------------------------------------ */
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_customer
WITH (LOCATION = 'dim_customer/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS customer_key, *
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, customer_unique_id, customer_city, customer_state, customer_zip_code_prefix
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_customers_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS c
) AS c;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   dim_seller
   One row per unique seller, same pattern as dim_customer above.
   ------------------------------------------------------------ */
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_seller
WITH (LOCATION = 'dim_seller/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY seller_id) AS seller_key, *
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT seller_id, seller_city, seller_state, seller_zip_code_prefix
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_sellers_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS s
) AS s;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   dim_product
   One row per unique product, enriched with the English
   translation of its category name (LEFT JOIN so a product keeps
   its row even if no translation match exists — its English
   category name would just come back NULL in that case).
   ------------------------------------------------------------ */
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_product
WITH (LOCATION = 'dim_product/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY product_id) AS product_key, *
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT p.product_id, p.product_category_name, t.product_category_name_english,
           p.product_weight_g, p.product_length_cm, p.product_height_cm, p.product_width_cm
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_products_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS p
    LEFT JOIN OPENROWSET(BULK 'product_category_name_translation', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS t
        ON p.product_category_name = t.product_category_name
) AS p;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   dim_date
   Full calendar dimension (2016-01-01 to 2018-12-31), pre-built
   in the Spark notebook and staged in Silver as 'dim_date_seed'.
   Unlike the other dimensions, this one does NOT get a
   ROW_NUMBER() surrogate key — its DateKey column (an integer in
   YYYYMMDD format, e.g. 20180315) already serves as a stable,
   human-readable surrogate key, which is standard practice for
   date dimensions in dimensional modeling.
   ------------------------------------------------------------ */
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE dim_date
WITH (
    LOCATION = 'dim_date/',
    DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake,
    FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff
)
AS
SELECT *
FROM OPENROWSET(
    BULK 'dim_date_seed/',
    DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake',
    FORMAT = 'DELTA'
) AS rows;

/* ============================================================
   GOLD LAYER — FACT TABLE
   Olist E-Commerce Analytics Project

   Purpose: builds fact_order_items, the central fact table of
   the star schema. Grain: one row per order line item (i.e. per
   product within an order — an order with 3 different products
   produces 3 rows here). Each row links out to every dimension
   via its surrogate key, and carries the numeric measures
   (price, freight, payment total, average review score).

   Must be run AFTER the dimension script, since this table
   joins against dim_customer, dim_product, dim_seller and
   dim_date to look up their surrogate keys.
   ============================================================ */

-- Database context is set by the pipeline's linked service (DBName = db_olist_gold);
-- uncomment the line below if running this script standalone in Synapse Studio.
-- USE db_olist_gold;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------
   Idempotent drop, same pattern as the dimension script: only
   drop if it exists (DROP EXTERNAL TABLE doesn't support
   IF EXISTS directly), so this script can be safely re-run by
   the automated pipeline.
   ------------------------------------------------------------ */
IF EXISTS (SELECT * FROM sys.external_tables WHERE name = 'fact_order_items')
    EXEC('DROP EXTERNAL TABLE fact_order_items');

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE fact_order_items
WITH (LOCATION = 'fact_order_items/', DATA_SOURCE = gold_lake, FILE_FORMAT = parquet_ff)
AS
SELECT
    -- Surrogate key for the fact table itself, ordered by the natural
    -- grain (order_id + order_item_id) so it's deterministic on every rebuild.
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY oi.order_id, oi.order_item_id) AS order_item_key,

    -- Foreign keys: translate each natural business key into its
    -- dimension's surrogate key via a join, rather than storing the
    -- natural key directly — keeps the fact table lean and consistent
    -- with standard Kimball star-schema design.
    dc.customer_key,
    dp.product_key,
    ds.seller_key,
    dd.date_key AS order_date_key,

    -- Degenerate dimensions / natural keys kept for traceability
    oi.order_id,
    oi.order_item_id,

    -- Measures
    oi.price,
    oi.freight_value,
    pay.total_payment_value,
    rev.avg_review_score

FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_order_items_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS oi

-- Orders table brought in purely to get customer_id and the purchase
-- timestamp — order_items itself doesn't carry those.
JOIN OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_orders_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS o
    ON oi.order_id = o.order_id

-- Dimension lookups (INNER JOIN — every order item should have a
-- valid customer/product/seller/date; a row silently disappearing
-- here would indicate a data quality issue worth investigating).
JOIN dim_customer dc ON o.customer_id = dc.customer_id
JOIN dim_product dp ON oi.product_id = dp.product_id
JOIN dim_seller ds ON oi.seller_id = ds.seller_id
JOIN dim_date dd ON CAST(o.order_purchase_timestamp AS DATE) = dd.Date

-- Payments: a single order can have multiple payment rows (e.g. split
-- across installments or payment methods), so we pre-aggregate to one
-- row per order_id BEFORE joining — otherwise the join would fan out
-- and duplicate every order_item row per payment record, silently
-- inflating price/freight totals downstream.
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(payment_value) AS total_payment_value
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_order_payments_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS p
    GROUP BY order_id
) pay ON oi.order_id = pay.order_id

-- Reviews: same fan-out concern as payments, plus TRY_CAST instead of
-- CAST — a single malformed/non-numeric review_score value would
-- otherwise fail the entire CETAS statement; TRY_CAST just returns
-- NULL for that one bad value instead, which AVG() then ignores.
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, AVG(TRY_CAST(review_score AS FLOAT)) AS avg_review_score
    FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'olist_order_reviews_dataset', DATA_SOURCE = 'silver_lake', FORMAT = 'DELTA') AS r
    GROUP BY order_id
) rev ON oi.order_id = rev.order_id;

CREATE USER [synw-olist-dev-weu] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
ALTER ROLE db_owner ADD MEMBER [synw-olist-dev-weu];

-- 1. Row counts — sanity check nothing is empty
SELECT 'dim_customer' AS TableName, COUNT(*) AS Rows FROM dim_customer
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_seller', COUNT(*) FROM dim_seller
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_product', COUNT(*) FROM dim_product
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_date', COUNT(*) FROM dim_date
UNION ALL SELECT 'fact_order_items', COUNT(*) FROM fact_order_items;

-- 2. Prove the joins actually work end to end
SELECT TOP 10
    c.customer_city,
    p.product_category_name,
    d.month_name,
    d.year,
    f.price
FROM fact_order_items f
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
JOIN dim_product  p ON f.product_key  = p.product_key
JOIN dim_date     d ON f.order_date_key = d.date_key;

# ============================================================
# BRONZE -> SILVER — DATA CLEANING
# Olist E-Commerce Analytics Project
#
# Purpose: reads each raw CSV from the Bronze container, applies
# real per-table cleaning logic (not just a CSV -> Delta format
# conversion), and writes the result to the Silver container as
# Delta tables. Each table has its own cleaning function tailored
# to its actual data quality issues, dispatched through the
# cleaning_functions dictionary at the bottom of this cell.
# ============================================================

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, trim, lower, upper, to_timestamp


def basic_clean(df):
    """
    Baseline cleaning applied to every table before its specific
    rules run: removes exact-duplicate rows, and trims stray
    leading/trailing whitespace from every string column (a common
    issue in CSV exports that can silently break joins and grouping
    later if left in).
    """
    df = df.dropDuplicates()
    for c, t in df.dtypes:
        if t == "string":
            df = df.withColumn(c, trim(col(c)))
    return df


def clean_orders(df):
    """
    Orders table: drops any row with a null order_id (a broken row
    with no usable primary key), standardizes order_status to
    lowercase for consistent filtering, and converts every date
    column from raw string/CSV format into a real timestamp type
    so downstream date math and joins to dim_date work correctly.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df)
    df = df.filter(col("order_id").isNotNull())
    df = df.withColumn("order_status", lower(trim(col("order_status"))))
    for ts_col in ["order_purchase_timestamp", "order_approved_at",
                   "order_delivered_carrier_date", "order_delivered_customer_date",
                   "order_estimated_delivery_date"]:
        df = df.withColumn(ts_col, to_timestamp(col(ts_col)))
    return df


def clean_order_items(df):
    """
    Order items table: the true uniqueness grain here is one row
    per (order_id, order_item_id) pair, so we dedup specifically on
    that combination rather than relying on exact full-row matches.
    Also filters out any row with a negative price or freight value
    — a negative amount is a data error, not a legitimate discount.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df)
    df = df.dropDuplicates(["order_id", "order_item_id"])
    df = df.filter((col("price") >= 0) & (col("freight_value") >= 0))
    return df


def clean_customers(df):
    """
    Customers table: deduplicated on customer_id (the true unique
    key), with state codes standardized to uppercase so "sp" and
    "SP" don't end up treated as two different states downstream.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df).dropDuplicates(["customer_id"])
    return df.withColumn("customer_state", upper(trim(col("customer_state"))))


def clean_sellers(df):
    """Sellers table: same dedup-and-standardize pattern as customers."""
    df = basic_clean(df).dropDuplicates(["seller_id"])
    return df.withColumn("seller_state", upper(trim(col("seller_state"))))


def clean_products(df):
    """
    Products table: fills missing product_category_name with the
    literal value "unknown" rather than leaving it null — this keeps
    the value groupable/filterable in reports instead of silently
    disappearing from category-based aggregations.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df)
    return df.fillna({"product_category_name": "unknown"})


def clean_order_payments(df):
    """Payments table: filters out any row with a negative payment_value (a data error)."""
    df = basic_clean(df)
    return df.filter(col("payment_value") >= 0)


def clean_order_reviews(df):
    """
    Reviews table: converts the two date columns to real timestamps,
    and dedups on (review_id, order_id) — the correct composite key,
    since a review_id alone isn't guaranteed unique across orders in
    the raw data.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df)
    df = df.withColumn("review_creation_date", to_timestamp(col("review_creation_date")))
    df = df.withColumn("review_answer_timestamp", to_timestamp(col("review_answer_timestamp")))
    df = df.dropDuplicates(["review_id", "order_id"])
    return df


def clean_geolocation(df):
    """
    Geolocation table: this is the noisiest raw dataset by far —
    basic_clean() alone removes a huge number of exact-duplicate
    rows, and the bounding-box filter below discards coordinates
    that fall well outside Brazil's actual borders (bad GPS data).
    Together these two steps cut this table's row count by roughly
    a quarter, which is the clearest evidence in this whole notebook
    that real cleaning — not just format conversion — is happening.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df)  # this alone removes a huge number of exact-duplicate rows
    return df.filter(col("geolocation_lat").between(-34, 6) &
                      col("geolocation_lng").between(-74, -32))  # rough Brazil bounding box


def clean_category_translation(df):
    """
    Category translation lookup table: both the Portuguese and
    English category name columns are lowercased and trimmed here
    so that the LEFT JOIN against this table in the Gold-layer
    dim_product build matches reliably, regardless of inconsistent
    casing in the source data.
    """
    df = basic_clean(df)
    df = df.withColumn("product_category_name", lower(trim(col("product_category_name"))))
    return df.withColumn("product_category_name_english", lower(trim(col("product_category_name_english"))))


# Dispatch table: maps each raw Bronze CSV file name to the specific
# cleaning function that knows how to handle its particular data
# quality issues. The main loop below drives entirely off this dict,
# so adding a new source table just means adding one new entry here.
cleaning_functions = {
    "olist_orders_dataset": clean_orders,
    "olist_order_items_dataset": clean_order_items,
    "olist_customers_dataset": clean_customers,
    "olist_sellers_dataset": clean_sellers,
    "olist_products_dataset": clean_products,
    "olist_order_payments_dataset": clean_order_payments,
    "olist_order_reviews_dataset": clean_order_reviews,   
    "olist_geolocation_dataset": clean_geolocation,
    "product_category_name_translation": clean_category_translation,
}

for file_name, clean_fn in cleaning_functions.items():

    # Drop any previously-registered table pointer first, so this
    # loop is safe to re-run from a clean state (mode("overwrite")
    # below handles the actual data replacement; this just prevents
    # a stale Spark table registration pointing at an old path).
    spark.sql(f"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS default.{file_name}")

    # Read the raw CSV straight from Bronze — inferSchema lets Spark
    # detect column types automatically from the data itself.
    raw_df = spark.read.option("header", "true").option("inferSchema", "true") \
        .csv(f"abfss://bronze@stolistdevweu.dfs.core.windows.net/{file_name}.csv")

    # Apply this table's specific cleaning function from the dict above.
    clean_df = clean_fn(raw_df)

    # Write to Silver as Delta. mode("overwrite") lets this cell be
    # re-run safely — Delta Lake replaces the previous version
    # atomically, no manual cleanup needed (unlike the Gold-layer
    # CETAS tables built later in SQL).
    clean_df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite") \
        .option("path", f"abfss://silver@stolistdevweu.dfs.core.windows.net/{file_name}") \
        .saveAsTable(file_name)

# ============================================================
# SILVER LAYER — DATE DIMENSION SEED
# Olist E-Commerce Analytics Project
#
# Purpose: generates a full calendar table (2016-01-01 through
# 2018-12-31 — covering the entire span of the Olist dataset)
# rather than deriving dates only from the ones that happen to
# appear in the orders data. A complete calendar means date-based
# reports (e.g. "revenue by month") never have gaps for days with
# zero orders, and supports future date-based analysis generically.
#
# This table is later picked up by the Gold-layer SQL script,
# which reads it via OPENROWSET and republishes it as dim_date
# in the gold container — this notebook only builds the Silver
# staging version.
# ============================================================

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Drop any previous version of the Spark table pointer before
# rewriting. Not strictly required since the write below uses
# overwrite mode anyway, but keeps this cell safe to re-run from
# a clean state if the table was ever registered at a different
# path in an earlier version of this script.
spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS default.dim_date_seed")

# 1. Generate one row per calendar day in the range.
#    explode(sequence(start, end, interval)) builds a single array
#    containing every date in the range, then explode() turns that
#    one array into one row per date — this is how a full calendar
#    gets generated without needing 1,096 rows of source data.
df_date = spark.sql("""
    SELECT explode(sequence(to_date('2016-01-01'), to_date('2018-12-31'), interval 1 day)) as Date
""")

# 2. Add descriptive columns used for filtering, grouping and
#    labeling in downstream reports (e.g. Power BI slicers/axes).
df_date = df_date \
    .withColumn("date_key", F.date_format("Date", "yyyyMMdd").cast("int")) \
    .withColumn("year", F.year("Date")) \
    .withColumn("quarter", F.quarter("Date")) \
    .withColumn("month", F.month("Date")) \
    .withColumn("month_name", F.date_format("Date", "MMMM")) \
    .withColumn("day_of_month", F.dayofmonth("Date")) \
    .withColumn("day_of_week", F.dayofweek("Date")) \
    .withColumn("day_name", F.date_format("Date", "EEEE")) \
    .withColumn("week_of_year", F.weekofyear("Date")) \
    .withColumn("is_weekend", F.when(F.dayofweek("Date").isin([1, 7]), 1).otherwise(0))

# Note on date_key: this yyyyMMdd integer (e.g. 20180315) doubles as
# the table's surrogate key. Unlike the other dimensions, no separate
# ROW_NUMBER() surrogate key is generated — a sortable, human-readable
# integer key is the standard, deliberate choice for date dimensions
# in dimensional modeling (see dim_date's comments in the Gold SQL
# script for the full reasoning).

# 3. Save into the silver container. mode("overwrite") means Delta
#    Lake handles replacing old data atomically and safely on every
#    re-run — no manual folder cleanup needed here, unlike the Gold
#    layer's CETAS tables, which have no equivalent overwrite option.
df_date.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite") \
    .option("path", "abfss://silver@stolistdevweu.dfs.core.windows.net/dim_date_seed") \
    .saveAsTable("dim_date_seed")

# nb_clear_gold — pipeline step that runs before the Gold SQL scripts.
# Serverless SQL's CETAS refuses to write into a non-empty folder, and
# DROP EXTERNAL TABLE only removes the SQL metadata, not the actual
# files — so this clears each table's Parquet folder in storage first.
# try/except keeps it safe to re-run even if a folder is already empty.
from notebookutils import mssparkutils

tables = ["dim_customer", "dim_seller", "dim_product", "dim_date", "fact_order_items"]

for t in tables:
    path = f"abfss://gold@stolistdevweu.dfs.core.windows.net/{t}/"
    try:
        mssparkutils.fs.rm(path, True)
        print(f"Deleted: {t}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Skipped {t} (likely already empty): {e}")
